sources.source_title: Scottish Referral Guidelines for Suspected Cancer: haematological cancers

background: Myeloma commonly presents with bone pain, anaemia symptoms, renal impairment symptoms, and hypercalcaemia symptoms.
MGUS is not cancer and is a common incidental finding in older people; the SRG cites progression to myeloma or related lymphoplasmacytic malignancy at around 1% per year.

history: Ask specifically about unexplained bone pain, particularly bony back pain, pathological or fragility fracture, fatigue, polyuria, polydipsia, peripheral neuropathy, and recurrent infection.
examination: Assess for signs of anaemia, dehydration, confusion, bone tenderness, neurological deficit, and features suggesting malignant spinal cord compression.
tests: For possible myeloma, particularly age 60 years or over, request FBC, plasma viscosity or ESR, renal function, and calcium.

If initial blood tests are suspicious or concern persists, request serum immunoglobulins, serum protein electrophoresis, serum free light chains, or urinary Bence Jones proteins if sFLC is not available.

red_flags.statement: Blood tests or imaging suggestive of myeloma with symptoms or signs of malignant spinal cord compression or acute kidney injury require same-day emergency referral.

Test results suggestive of myeloma, including raised paraprotein concentrations, paraprotein bands, abnormal sFLC or urinary Bence Jones proteins, plus at least one CRAB feature require urgent suspicion of cancer referral.

primary_care_management: If blood tests are normal, myeloma is unlikely; investigate other causes while safety-netting and repeating baseline tests if symptoms remain concerning and unexplained.
Do not refer raised paraprotein alone as USC when there are no additional USC features; follow local non-USC or primary-care management guidance.

usoc: Raised paraprotein concentration, paraprotein band, abnormal sFLC or urinary Bence Jones protein with one or more CRAB criteria.
routine: Raised paraprotein without CRAB features should follow local non-USC haematology or primary-care management pathways.

do_not_refer: Do not use USC for lymphocytosis or raised paraprotein without the additional features in the referral criteria.

evidence_index.statement: Initial myeloma tests: FBC, plasma viscosity or ESR, renal function, calcium.
thresholds: Age 60 years or over strengthens suspicion but does not exclude younger adults
evidence_index.population: Adults with unexplained features suggestive of myeloma

evidence_index.statement: Further tests include serum immunoglobulins, serum protein electrophoresis, serum free light chains, or urinary Bence Jones proteins if sFLC unavailable.
thresholds: Suspicious initial blood tests or ongoing clinical concern

evidence_index.statement: USC referral for results suggestive of myeloma plus one or more CRAB criteria.
Same-day emergency referral for myeloma-suggestive tests or imaging with malignant spinal cord compression features or acute kidney injury.
Raised paraprotein without USC features should not be referred as USC.
evidence_index.uncertainty: Local non-USC pathway threshold still needs D&G haematology confirmation.

access.notes: Relevant recommendation text extracted; guideline is mainly secondary-care focused.

tests: Use serum protein electrophoresis and serum-free light-chain assay to confirm paraprotein indicating possible myeloma or MGUS.
If serum protein electrophoresis is abnormal, use serum immunofixation to confirm the paraprotein.
Do not use serum protein electrophoresis, serum immunofixation, serum-free light-chain assay, or urine electrophoresis alone to exclude myeloma.

primary_care_management: People with myeloma should be advised how to identify and report new symptoms, especially pain and spinal cord compression symptoms.
medicines: Specialist myeloma treatment and bone disease medicines are outside primary-care initiation scope.
scope_gaps: NG35 does not provide primary-care MGUS follow-up thresholds.

evidence_index.statement: Serum protein electrophoresis plus serum-free light-chain assay confirms paraprotein indicating possible myeloma or MGUS.
evidence_index.population: People with suspected myeloma or MGUS

evidence_index.statement: Abnormal serum protein electrophoresis should be followed by serum immunofixation.
evidence_index.population: People with suspected myeloma or MGUS

evidence_index.statement: Do not use a single negative paraprotein or light-chain test alone to exclude myeloma.

history: Persistent bone pain or unexplained fracture in people aged 60 and over should prompt initial myeloma blood tests.
tests: The April 2025 NG12 update amended myeloma blood-test recommendations and added serum protein electrophoresis into the initial diagnostic approach.
Offer FBC, calcium, and either plasma viscosity or ESR in people aged 60 and over with persistent bone pain or unexplained fracture.
If raised plasma viscosity or ESR is consistent with possible myeloma, arrange urgent protein electrophoresis and Bence Jones protein testing; sFLC may be used where available.

scope_gaps: Direct NICE NG12 myeloma subsection was not cleanly isolated by the web extractor.

evidence_index.statement: For age 60 and over with persistent bone pain or unexplained fracture, initial tests include FBC, calcium, and plasma viscosity or ESR.
evidence_index.population: Adults with symptoms suggestive of myeloma
evidence_index.uncertainty: Direct NG12 page extraction was broad; statement is supported by NICE-linked update summary.

evidence_index.statement: If inflammatory marker results support possible myeloma, urgent protein electrophoresis and Bence Jones protein or sFLC testing should follow.
thresholds: Raised plasma viscosity or ESR consistent with possible myeloma
evidence_index.uncertainty: Direct NG12 page extraction was broad; statement is supported by NICE-linked update summary.

background: MGUS is defined by monoclonal protein without organ damage typical of myeloma or related malignancy.
Risk stratification should guide monitoring intensity and whether secondary-care assessment is needed.

history: Ask about myeloma/MGCS symptoms: bone pain, fractures, fatigue, recurrent infection, neuropathy, renal symptoms, weight loss, and symptoms of AL amyloidosis where relevant.
tests: For MGUS monitoring, use paraprotein trend, FBC, renal function, calcium, and sFLC where indicated.

primary_care_management: Low-risk IgG MGUS with paraprotein <15 g/L and normal sFLC ratio may be monitored in primary care after initial stability check, depending on local policy.
Repeat monitoring around 6 months after diagnosis to establish stability, then reduce frequency if stable.
Consider stopping routine surveillance for low-risk MGUS in people over 80 years or with life expectancy under 5 years after shared decision-making.

urgent: Refer for haematology assessment if IgG paraprotein is >15 g/L, IgA or IgM paraprotein is >10 g/L, sFLC ratio is outside 0.1 to 7, or paraprotein rises by >25% and >5 g/L from baseline.
routine: Stable low-risk MGUS can usually remain under primary-care monitoring if no symptoms, no CRAB features, and no significant paraprotein or sFLC change.

do_not_refer: Do not refer stable low-risk MGUS urgently in the absence of symptoms, CRAB features, significant paraprotein rise, or markedly abnormal sFLC ratio.
scope_gaps: D&G local haematology should confirm exact primary-care monitoring interval and non-urgent referral route.

evidence_index.statement: Low-risk IgG MGUS is IgG paraprotein <15 g/L with normal sFLC ratio and can be monitored in primary care after stability check.
evidence_index.population: Adults with MGUS and no myeloma-defining features
evidence_index.uncertainty: Full paper PDF extraction limited; confirm with local haematology before publication.

evidence_index.statement: Initial MGUS monitoring is around 6 months after diagnosis, then less frequent if stable.
Refer if IgG paraprotein >15 g/L, IgA or IgM paraprotein >10 g/L, sFLC ratio outside 0.1 to 7, or paraprotein rises by >25% and >5 g/L.
evidence_index.uncertainty: Full paper PDF extraction limited; confirm with local haematology before publication.

evidence_index.statement: Consider stopping routine low-risk MGUS surveillance in people over 80 years or life expectancy under 5 years after shared decision-making.

background: MGUS is not cancer, usually has no symptoms, and does not require treatment.
Myeloma UK describes MGUS as affecting about 1 in 30 people over 50, 1 in 20 over 70, and nearly 1 in 10 over 85.
Over 10 years, about 10% of people with MGUS develop myeloma.

history: Patients should report fatigue, pain, recurrent or frequent infections, and fractures.
tests: MGUS monitoring looks at trends in blood results and symptoms.

primary_care_management: MGUS is actively monitored, not treated.
Monitoring is commonly every 3 to 4 months for the first year after diagnosis, then every 6 to 12 months if no symptoms develop.

evidence_index.statement: MGUS is not cancer, usually asymptomatic, and does not require treatment.
MGUS checks are commonly every 3 to 4 months for the first year, then every 6 to 12 months if stable and asymptomatic.
thresholds: Every 3 to 4 months for first year
evidence_index.uncertainty: Patient-facing source; BSH/UKMS suggests less intensive follow-up for low-risk MGUS in some cases.

evidence_index.statement: Patients should report fatigue, pain, recurrent or frequent infections, and fractures.
